sec.title: Aims
sec.p: To evaluate the effect of UGT1A1*28 homozygosity on the safety profile of NALIRIFOX (liposomal irinotecan + 5-fluorouracil/leucovorin + oxaliplatin) in patients with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (mPDAC) in NAPOLI 3 (NCT04083235).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This pre-specified exploratory analysis evaluated safety outcomes by UGT1A1*28 status in patients with mPDAC receiving NALIRIFOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel in NAPOLI 3. All patients receiving NALIRIFOX initiated liposomal irinotecan at the full starting dose.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 749 treated patients, 83 were homozygous for UGT1A1*28. In the NALIRIFOX arm, grade ≥3 and serious treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) related to liposomal irinotecan occurred in 61.5% and 33.3% of patients with homozygous UGT1A1*28 (n = 39), respectively, compared with 63.7% and 22.9% of patients with other genotypes (n = 328). The most common any-grade TEAEs for NALIRIFOX were diarrhea (59.0%), nausea (56.4%), vomiting (46.2%), and anemia (41.0%) in the homozygous group and diarrhea (71.6%), nausea (59.8%), vomiting (38.4%), and decreased appetite (38.1%) in the other genotypes group. Rates of TEAE-related treatment discontinuation and dose reduction/interruption in the NALIRIFOX arm were similar across genotypes.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: UGT1A1*28 homozygosity was not associated with increased toxicity in patients receiving NALIRIFOX in NAPOLI 3. These findings support the use of full NALIRIFOX dosing irrespective of UGT1A1*28 status.

abstract.title: Plain Language Summary
abstract.p: Irinotecan is a drug used to treat people with pancreatic cancer. Some people have two copies of a gene type called UGT1A1*28 that can make it harder for their bodies to handle irinotecan. When doctors use regular irinotecan in people with two UGT1A1*28 copies, they often use a lower drug dose to reduce the risk of treatment side-effects. A version of irinotecan called liposomal irinotecan has been developed to offer potential benefits over regular irinotecan. We wanted to investigate the safety of using liposomal irinotecan in people with two UGT1A1*28 copies. We used data from a study called NAPOLI 3. In this study, people with pancreatic cancer received either NALIRIFOX (a drug combination containing liposomal irinotecan) or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel. Of the 749 patients in the trial, 83 had two UGT1A1*28 copies, and 39 of these patients received full-dose liposomal irinotecan as part of their NALIRIFOX treatment. We checked the side-effects of liposomal irinotecan treatment in patients with and without two UGT1A1*28 copies. The most common side-effects of liposomal irinotecan were diarrhea and feeling or being sick. We found that having two copies of the UGT1A1*28 gene type had no effect on the risk of side-effects to liposomal irinotecan. Overall, we found that having two UGT1A1*28 copies should not affect the dose of liposomal irinotecan given to patients. This is important because irinotecan treatment at the full recommended dose has the best chance to work well.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Worldwide, pancreatic cancer is the sixth leading cause of cancer mortality and is responsible for 5% of all cancer deaths [1]. Patients with a diagnosis of metastatic disease have an estimated 5-year survival of 3% [2]. With the emergence of novel therapies targeting pancreatic cancers with specific gene alterations (including zenocutuzumab-zbco for patients with neuregulin 1 gene fusions [3] and entrectinib for patients with neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase gene fusions [4]) comes the promise of a more-individualized treatment landscape for pancreatic cancer. Currently, however, chemotherapy remains the mainstay of treatment.

In 2024, liposomal irinotecan (Onivyde®) in combination with 5-fluorouracil/leucovorin and oxaliplatin (NALIRIFOX) was approved in Europe and the USA for the first-line treatment of adults with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (mPDAC) [5,6]. Approval was based on the results of the phase III NAPOLI 3 trial (Clinical trial registration September 2019: www.clinicaltrials.gov identifier is NCT04083235), in which first-line NALIRIFOX demonstrated clinically meaningful and statistically significant treatment benefits compared with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (Gem+NabP) in patients with mPDAC (median overall survival 11.1 vs 9.2 months, respectively [hazard ratio 0.83 [95% CI, 0.70–0.99]; p = 0.036], and median progression-free survival 7.4 vs 5.6 months, respectively [hazard ratio 0.69 [95% CI, 0.58–0.83]; p < 0.0001]) [7].

Irinotecan is a topoisomerase I inhibitor that is converted to its active metabolite, SN-38, which is 100- to 1000-fold more potent than irinotecan [8]. SN-38 is cleared by the liver enzyme uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) and biliary excretion [9]. Variations in thymine–adenine-repeat length within the UGT1A1 promoter sequence affect UGT1A1 activity [9]; the UGT1A1*28 polymorphism contains seven thymine–adenine repeats [10] leading to reduced gene expression and thereby enzymatic activity [9]. Homozygosity for UGT1A1*28 can lead to elevated SN-38 exposure, increasing the risk of toxicity in patients receiving irinotecan-based treatment [9].

Liposomal irinotecan differs from conventional irinotecan (non-liposomal irinotecan) by using a liposomal drug-delivery system that stabilizes irinotecan within long-circulating liposomes, allowing controlled release and higher in vivo stability than non-liposomal irinotecan [11,12]. This formulation alters pharmacokinetics compared with non-liposomal irinotecan, potentially reducing variability in SN-38 exposure associated with UGT1A1*28 homozygosity.

Dosing guidance for non-liposomal irinotecan, a component of the FOLFIRINOX regimen, indicates that reduced starting doses should be considered for patients who are homozygous for UGT1A1*28 [13]. A population pharmacokinetic analysis based on seven clinical trials (including the phase III NAPOLI-1 trial) suggested that the UGT1A1*28 polymorphism has no significant impact on the pharmacokinetics of liposomal irinotecan, with no need for dose adjustments based on the UGT1A1*28 genotype [14]. An updated population pharmacokinetic analysis (including data from NAPOLI 3) confirmed this conclusion [6].

Here, we report the results of a pre-specified exploratory analysis of the impact of UGT1A1*28 homozygosity on the incidence and profile of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) in the NAPOLI 3 trial population.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: NAPOLI 3 was a randomized, open-label, phase III study conducted at 187 sites in 18 countries (Figure 1); detailed methods for the overall trial have been reported previously [7]. Briefly, adults (aged ≥18 years) with previously untreated mPDAC and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status score of 0 or 1 were randomly assigned to receive NALIRIFOX (liposomal irinotecan 50 mg/m2, leucovorin 400 mg/m2, fluorouracil 2400 mg/m2, and oxaliplatin 60 mg/m2, administered sequentially as a continuous intravenous infusion over 46 h) on days 1 and 15 of a 28-day cycle or Gem+NabP (gemcitabine 1000 mg/m2 and nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m2), administered intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day cycle. The primary endpoint was overall survival in the intention-to treat population, and safety was evaluated in all patients who received at least one dose of study treatment.

sec.p: The study was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Conference on Harmonisation Consolidated Guideline on Good Clinical Practice, and the requirements of the US Food and Drug Administration or local regulatory authorities regarding the conduct of human clinical trials. The protocol was approved by the local institutional review board and independent ethics committees of the participating centers. A full list of the local institutional review boards and independent ethics committees is provided in Supplementary Table S1. Signed informed consent forms were obtained for each participant prior to any study procedure being conducted.

The exploratory endpoint of this pre-specified analysis of the NAPOLI 3 data was safety according to UGT1A1*28 status (homozygous vs other genotypes [heterozygous or wild-type]). UGT1A1*28 status was evaluated in all patients prior to enrollment, and all patients received the full starting dose of liposomal irinotecan and followed the same dose-reduction protocol.

sec.title: Endpoints and statistical analysis
sec.p: This exploratory analysis was descriptive in nature, and was not powered for formal statistical comparisons between genotype groups. Analyses were performed on all randomly assigned patients who received at least one dose of study treatment (safety population). The number and proportion of participants and safety outcomes by UGT1A1*28 status were summarized descriptively.

Adverse events were coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 25.0, and toxicity was graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: The baseline characteristics of patients who were randomized in NAPOLI 3 (N = 770) were balanced between treatment groups (Table 1) [7]. In the NALIRIFOX (n = 383) and Gem+NabP (n = 387) arms, respectively, 204 (53.3%) and 230 (59.4%) patients were male; median age was 64.0 and 65.0 years; 160 (41.8%) and 168 (43.4%) patients had an ECOG performance status of 0; 149 (38.9%) and 141 (36.4%) patients had three or more metastatic sites, and 307 (80.2%) and 311 (80.4%) patients had liver metastases. Regarding UGT1A1 genotype, 40 (10.4%) and 45 (11.6%) patients in the two arms, respectively, were homozygous for UGT1A1*28.

sec.title: Safety outcomes
sec.p: The incidence of any TEAEs, grade ≥3 TEAEs, and TEAEs leading to death, was consistent between the UGT1A1*28 homozygous group and other genotypes group, in both the NALIRIFOX and Gem+NabP arms of the trial (Table 3). Grade ≥3 TEAEs related to liposomal irinotecan in the NALIRIFOX arm were experienced by 24/39 patients who were UGT1A1*28 homozygous (61.5%) and by 209/328 patients with other genotypes (63.7%). Serious TEAEs related to liposomal irinotecan were reported for 13/39 (33.3%) and 75/328 (22.9%) patients in the two genotype groups, respectively.

sec.p: There was one death related to liposomal irinotecan (due to pancytopenia) in the UGT1A1*28 homozygous group and there were five deaths related to liposomal irinotecan in the other genotypes group (due to febrile neutropenia, ischemic stroke, peritumoural edema, general physical health deterioration, and sepsis [n = 1 each]).

TEAEs of any grade and grade 3–4 are summarized in Figure 2 for patients who received NALIRIFOX stratified by UGT1A1*28 status. The most frequently reported any-grade TEAEs in this group were diarrhea (23/39, 59.0%), nausea (22/39, 56.4%), vomiting (18/39, 46.2%), and anemia (16/39, 41.0%) for those who were homozygous for UGT1A1*28, and diarrhea (235/328, 71.6%), nausea (196/328, 59.8%), vomiting (126/328, 38.4%), and decreased appetite (125/328, 38.1%), for those in the other genotypes group.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This pre-specified exploratory analysis assessed the impact of UGT1A1*28 homozygosity on the incidence and profile of TEAEs in NAPOLI 3. There was no evidence to suggest increased toxicity in patients with UGT1A1*28 homozygosity, in either arm of the trial. The incidence of TEAEs, including TEAEs leading to death, was similar between the UGT1A1*28 homozygous group and other genotypes group. The profile of TEAEs was consistent with that reported for the overall NAPOLI 3 safety population [7].

This is the first report of the impact of UGT1A1*28 status on the safety profile of the NALIRIFOX chemotherapy regimen. The result of this analysis supports the findings of a population pharmacokinetic analysis based on data from eight clinical trials (including the phase III NAPOLI-1 trial), which suggested that there was no need for dose adjustments based on the UGT1A1*28 genotype [6,14]. Liposomal encapsulation of irinotecan in NALIRIFOX eliminates the need for the dose reductions required by some patients receiving non-liposomal irinotecan in FOLFIRINOX. Although a modified FOLFIRINOX (mFOLFIRINOX) regimen with irinotecan dosed at 150 mg/m2 is available, conventional 180 mg/m2 irinotecan dosing in FOLFIRINOX continues to be widely used, particularly for the treatment of patients with locally advanced and metastatic disease. Whether UGT1A1*28 homozygosity results in the requirement for further dose reductions beyond 150 mg/m2 when using mFOLFIRINOX remains unexplored. In contrast, NALIRIFOX allows delivery of the full liposomal irinotecan dose without the preemptive reductions often applied in mFOLFIRINOX.

UGT1A1*28 status had no apparent impact on the safety profile of NALIRIFOX. However, judicious dosing (guided by performance status and clinical parameters) and appropriate adverse event management strategies to address side effects such as diarrhea remain critical to optimizing treatment benefit for all patients with mPDAC. In recognition of the prevalence of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) in patients with mPDAC, a relevant consideration when devising effective mitigation strategies for gastrointestinal adverse events induced by systemic mPDAC therapy is assessment and management of underlying PEI, regardless of a patient's UGT1A1*28 status. These findings may inform future UGT1A1*28 testing protocols for treatment with NALIRIFOX.

Potential confounders, including ECOG performance status, metastatic burden, hepatic involvement, baseline bilirubin, PEI, and supportive care, could also influence toxicity profiles and dose management. Importantly, UGT1A1*28 status was not a stratification factor in NAPOLI 3, so these variables may have contributed to observed safety outcomes. Future analyses should consider multivariate approaches to better isolate the effect of UGT1A1*28 from these factors. A further limitation is lack of data on UGT1A1*6 genotype, a polymorphism that is also known to affect UGT1A1 enzymatic activity [15].

The analysis aimed to address a recognized safety consideration when treating patients with irinotecan-based regimens. Its findings were strengthened by its use of robust phase III clinical trial data and by the fact that, because UGT1A1*28 status was not a randomization factor in NAPOLI 3, the baseline characteristics for each study arm were well balanced between the homozygous group and other genotypes group. However, the exploratory nature of this pre-specified analysis, the open-label design of NAPOLI 3, and the small number of patients with homozygous UGT1A1*28 status should be taken into consideration when interpreting the data as the analysis may be underpowered to detect differences in safety outcomes or rare events between UGT1A1 subgroups.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: UGT1A1*28 homozygosity did not increase the risk of toxicity in patients receiving liposomal irinotecan as part of the NALIRIFOX regimen. Unlike non-liposomal irinotecan-based regimens, these findings support the use of full NALIRIFOX dosing irrespective of UGT1A1*28 status.

list-item.p: Although chemotherapy remains the mainstay of first‑line treatment, metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (mPDAC) continues to be associated with poor survival.

NALIRIFOX (liposomal irinotecan plus 5‑fluorouracil/leucovorin and oxaliplatin) is an approved first‑line regimen for mPDAC based on improved survival outcomes versus Gem+NabP in the phase III NAPOLI 3 trial.
UGT1A1*28 homozygosity is a recognized risk factor for increased toxicity with non‑liposomal irinotecan, for which dosing guidelines recommend a reduced starting dose.

The liposomal formulation of irinotecan modifies pharmacokinetics relative to non‑liposomal irinotecan, potentially reducing genotype‑related variability in exposure to SN‑38, the active metabolite of irinotecan.
This pre‑specified exploratory analysis of NAPOLI 3 evaluated the safety of NALIRIFOX according to UGT1A1*28 genotype.
UGT1A1*28 homozygosity was not associated with increased toxicity of NALIRIFOX, including grade ≥3 adverse events, serious adverse events, or treatment discontinuation.
The safety profile and dose‑modification rates were similar across genotype groups, indicating that UGT1A1*28 status did not adversely affect tolerability or dose delivery.
These findings support initiation of full‑dose NALIRIFOX irrespective of UGT1A1*28 genotype.
